script: My flight crew vanished mid‑air—was it sabotage, betrayal, or a hidden trap?. The jet landed, refueled, and then… an external tank blew a fuse. We were told we'd need a defueling truck, but the Spanish base said we'd have to sample the fuel, send it to a lab, and wait days. (I know, right?) They'd promised us a quick 20‑minute swap, not a whole‑blowout of logistics. Then the commander, like, "burn the fuel if it's that important." We didn't need a second "burn it" because we were already losing a jet for days. Morning at 5:30 a.male.—the base was dead quiet. Four of us were already strolling the runway, sun still a pale bruise on the horizon. Suddenly two engines roared to life. We slammed the throttle to the max, the brakes gave out, and the asphalt blistered. Dust, sand, and the jet's own fuel erupted into a cloud that shot straight into an open Spanish Air Force shelter. Twenty‑five minutes later, 1,700 kilograms of fuel had turned into a crater of fire. The external tank was swapped out, and by 7:00 a.male. the jet was back on the runway, ready for the day's missions. The Spanish base commander had to meet our CO to figure out who'd woken him up so early. Two hours of sweeping followed, all while we explained the whole "fuel sampling" fiasco. Finally, they lifted the restriction: we could use the defueling truck without a lab sample. We never needed it again, but that liaison officer? He ended up in a long meeting with the base commander. If there hadn't been jets launching, you'd have heard the commander yelling all the way down the runway. (Literally insane.)
